# 2.1 - Standard Deviation {.unnumbered}

Two basketball players both score **10 points** per game on average.

![](/images/Unit_2/2.1_players.svg){width="560px" fig-align="center"}

Player A scores close to 10 every game. Player B might score 2 or 18. The mean is the same, but the players are very different.

In this lesson, you learn the {{< glink "standard deviation" >}}, a number that measures this spread.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I explain what the standard deviation tells about data.
- [ ] I find the standard deviation of a small data set.
- [ ] I compare the spread of data sets by looking at graphs.
:::

### 2.1.1 - What the SD Tells You

The {{< glink "standard deviation" >}} (SD) is about **how far the values usually are from the mean**.

- **Small SD:** the values are close to the mean.
- **Large SD:** the values are spread out.

Player A has a small SD. Player B has a large SD.

***

### 2.1.2 - Finding the Standard Deviation

**Example:** 7, 7, 10, 13, 13

| Step | Work |
|---|---|
| 1. Find the mean, $\bar{x}$. | $\bar{x} = 50 \div 5 = 10$ |
| 2. Subtract the mean from each value. | See the table below. |
| 3. Square each result. | See the table below. |
| 4. Add the squares. | $\Sigma(x - \bar{x})^2 = 9 + 9 + 0 + 9 + 9 = 36$ |
| 5. Divide by $n - 1$. This is the {{< glink variance >}}. | $36 \div 4 = 9$ |
| 6. Take the square root. | $s = \sqrt{9} = 3$ |

| $x$ | $x - \bar{x}$ | $(x - \bar{x})^2$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 7 | $-3$ | 9 |
| 7 | $-3$ | 9 |
| 10 | 0 | 0 |
| 13 | 3 | 9 |
| 13 | 3 | 9 |
| | $\Sigma(x - \bar{x})^2$ | **36** |

The standard deviation is $s = 3$.

:::{.remember title="The Formula"}
$$
s = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}
$$

- $\Sigma$ (capital **sigma**) means **add up**.
- $\Sigma(x - \bar{x})^2$ means: find $(x - \bar{x})^2$ for every value, then add them all.
- $n$ is how many values there are.
- $s$ is the standard deviation.
:::

:::{.think title="Why divide by n − 1 and not n?"}
Our data is usually a {{< glink sample >}}, a small part of a bigger group.

A sample is usually a little less spread out than the whole group. Dividing by $n - 1$ makes $s$ a little bigger. This fixes the problem.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Find the SD of 2, 4, 6"}
Mean: $12 \div 3 = 4$.

Differences: $-2, 0, 2$. Squares: $4, 0, 4$. So $\Sigma(x - \bar{x})^2 = 8$.

$s = \sqrt{8 \div 2} = \sqrt{4} = 2$
:::

***

### 2.1.3 - Facts About the SD

:::{.remember title="Facts About the Standard Deviation"}
- The SD is **never negative**.
- The SD is **0** only when every value is the same.
- The SD has the **same units** as the data (points, minutes, inches).
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Finding the SD**

1. Find the standard deviation of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.

2. Four quiz scores: 7, 3, 7, 7. Find the standard deviation.

3. Look at the two players at the top of this page.

   Player A: 9, 10, 10, 11, 10

   Player B: 2, 18, 5, 15, 10

   a. Find the mean of each player.

   b. Without calculating, which player has the larger SD? Explain.

   c. Find $s$ for Player A.

   d. Player B's SD is about 6.67. A coach needs a player who scores close to 10 points every game. Which player should the coach choose? Explain.
